summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark comparisons between Redwood (hosted + dedicated configs) and the customer's baseline provider. Discussed p50/p95 latency, throughput, batching/kv caching and quantization tradeoffs. Redwood showed improved p95 latency and higher throughput in dedicated config vs baseline. Customers raised questions about tail latency, accuracy impact of quantization, and security/SOC2 artifacts. Agreed next steps: share raw logs/spreadsheet, propose tuning configs, supply traffic sample, and schedule on-prem dry-run.
transcript:
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samir from Redwood here, Jenna our SE is on as well. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya Chen: Maya here. Roberto and Alicia on.
[00:12] Roberto Diaz: Roberto, SRE.
[00:14] Alicia Park: Alicia, CTO.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Great. Agenda: quick recap of last week, run through the benchmark spreadsheet, discuss tuning levers, and assign next steps. Jenna, you wanna kick with the numbers?
[00:27] Jenna Liu: Yeah sure. So we ran three main runs this week — baseline provider (what you sent), Redwood hosted default, and Redwood dedicated with batching and kv cache enabled plus int8 quant profile. I'll just call out the headline numbers first.
[00:40] Jenna Liu: Baseline p50 120ms p95 460ms throughput about 120 reqs per second on your sample. Redwood hosted (default) p50 95ms p95 320ms throughput 150 rps. Dedicated tuned run p50 70ms p95 240ms throughput 180 rps. Token cost estimates: baseline roughly $0.006 per token on average, Redwood hosted $0.005, Redwood dedicated after batching/kv/quant ~ $0.0038.
[01:12] Maya Chen: Those are promising numbers for dedicated. One quick question, how are you measuring p95 — is it end-to-end including network and TLS, or just inference time?
[01:22] Jenna Liu: Good question — we included end-to-end from request ingress at our edge to token stream start. So TLS, routing, everything. In the raw logs I can break out the kernel time only if you want.
[01:31] Roberto Diaz: When you say kv cache enabled — are you doing prefix caching per session? Our workload is somewhat conversational but most calls have similar prefixes.
[01:39] Jenna Liu: Yes, prefix caching on warm sessions. The benchmark included a mix: 60% repeated prefixes, 40% cold. That's why dedicated shows much better p95 — cache hit rate increased effective throughput.
[01:49] Alicia Park: Any sign of quality degradation with int8? We cannot accept hallucinations creeping in.
[01:54] Jenna Liu: We ran our eval on the held-out prompt set you provided — there was a tiny delta in exact-match metrics, like 0.7% drop on the rouge/f1 proxy we used, mostly on long-tail arithmetic snippets. For typical assistant-style completions the difference was negligible. We'll attach the eval CSV.
[02:10] Maya Chen: Could you repeat the raw latency numbers with units? I think I missed the p95 for hosted.
[02:15] Samir Patel: Hosted p95 was ~320ms, dedicated ~240ms, baseline ~460ms.
[02:21] Maya Chen: Ok got it.
[02:23] Roberto Diaz: For throughput numbers, is that requests per second at concurrency 50 or 200? We run big spikes during 10am and 2pm.
[02:31] Jenna Liu: Throughput numbers are at concurrency 100 in the benchmark harness. We can run spike tests at 500 concurrency to simulate your peak.
[02:36] Alicia Park: Do you have tail-latency histograms? P95 is useful but we care about p99 and the long tail.
[02:42] Jenna Liu: Yes — p99 for dedicated was 420ms, hosted p99 about 700ms, baseline p99 ~980ms. The big contributors to p99 are cold model loads and occasional GC pauses on the baseline infra; our runtime isolates background compactions so we see fewer long tails.
[02:58] Maya Chen: Interesting. The p99 difference is material. What about cold starts — how long if a model is cold?
[03:04] Jenna Liu: Cold-start to first token for our dedicated environment is about 1.8s for large weights (first request). Hosted cold start can be 2.5–3s depending on GPU warming. Baseline reported 3.5–4s in your logs. We also use pinned warm pools for critical routes to get that under 1s if needed.
[03:21] Roberto Diaz: Regarding security, Alicia had a question on KMS — can keys be customer managed?
[03:26] Samir Patel: Yes — for Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations. We also produce audit logs per request and have SOC2 artifacts; Jenna will drop the security pack.
[03:35] Alicia Park: Good. Also need to confirm network setup for private — VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink?
[03:40] Jenna Liu: Both are options. For on-prem we do a control-plane/out-of-band flow and the inference plane stays in your network. We can draft a diagram.
[03:47] Maya Chen: Back to tuning: what was the batch size you used for dedicated?
[03:51] Jenna Liu: Effective micro-batch was 8 with dynamic batching up to 32 when concurrency spikes; we tuned the queue time threshold to 10ms to keep latency low. For hosted defaults it was more conservative.
[03:59] Roberto Diaz: You mentioned kv cache policy — what eviction strategy?
[04:02] Jenna Liu: LRU with session affinity. We can make it TTL-based too. For your prompts we saw a 62% cache hit in the mixed workload.
[04:10] Maya Chen: On accuracy, can we get the eval diffs per prompt? I want to see which prompts degrade under int4 or int8 quant.
[04:16] Jenna Liu: Absolutely — I'll include the per-prompt CSV and a small summary of failure modes.
[04:20] Samir Patel: Also worth noting cost tradeoffs — when you amortize model cost across cached tokens and batching, dedicated can get to ~35–40% lower per-token cost than the baseline on your profile.
[04:30] Alicia Park: If we go dedicated reserved, what's the commit term?
[04:33] Samir Patel: Standard is monthly or annual committed capacity. We can sketch a 6-month pilot pricing as well if you want lower friction.
[04:40] Roberto Diaz: One blocker for us is whether logs include user PII — we need to ensure logs can be redacted and we can opt out of any long-term retention.
[04:48] Jenna Liu: That's supported. You can set retention policies per customer and we redact sensitive fields on ingestion; the audit logs we deliver can be minimal or full depending on contract.
[04:56] Maya Chen: Great. Any surprises in the raw logs?
[04:59] Jenna Liu: One thing — we saw a subset of requests with repeated re-try patterns from the baseline harness which inflated baseline p99; those were client-side retries every 200ms. We filtered that out for the main comparison but we'll share both filtered and unfiltered numbers.
[05:12] Samir Patel: Ok, let's recap next steps: I'll drop the benchmark sheet and raw logs, Jenna will send the per-prompt evals and tuning config. Maya to provide the traffic sample. We'll schedule an on-prem dry-run week of Oct 12th. Anything else?
[05:26] Alicia Park: Please include the SOC2 and KMS integration docs in the package.
[05:29] Samir Patel: Will do.
[05:31] Maya Chen: Also I want to run a spike test at concurrency 500 to validate throttling — can you run that?
[05:36] Jenna Liu: Yes we'll run spike tests and include results in the folder.
[05:39] Samir Patel: Cool. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts by end of week.
[05:44] Roberto Diaz: Thanks.
[05:46] Alicia Park: Bye.
[05:48] [meeting end]
